brave-llmcontext.snippet:
## Models
Models in COPASI are based on *reactions* that convert a set of *species* into another set of *species*. Each *species* is located in a *compartment*, which is a physical location with a size (volume, area, etc). This maps directly to biochemical reaction networks, but can also represent other types of processes (for example, the species could be cell types). COPASI automatically converts the reaction network to a set of differential equations or to a system of stochastic reaction events — the user does not have to write down the math explicitly, the software does that.
## Analysis
- Stoichiometric analysis of the reaction network, including *mass conservation analysis* and *elementary flux modes*.
- Optimization of arbitrary components of the model using a range of diverse algorithms.
- Parameter estimation using a range of diverse optimization algorithms. This can be done over several different experiments simultaneously, including mixtures of steady-state and time course experiments.
- Local sensitivity analysis.
- Metabolic control analysis (a special form of sensitivity analysis).
- Time scale separation analysis; this allows definition of fast and slow components of the model, in a time-dependent way.

Examine how modular skill-based design enables AI to reliably execute complex biochemical modeling workflows through COPASI and Basico.

COPASI Skills is an open-source framework designed to automate and standardize complex biochemical modeling workflows by providing AI agents with structured instructions to operate the COmplex PAthway SImulator (COPASI) via the Basico Python interface. The project addresses the challenge of making robust modeling procedures—such as parameter estimation, sensitivity analysis, and metabolic control analysis (MCA)—accessible to AI assistants in a repeatable and reliable manner.

### Core Methodology and Software Design

This document covers the optimization and computational analysis tasks available in basico, focusing on general optimization problems, steady-state analysis, sensitivity analysis, and specialized mathematical analysis methods. These tasks enable users to optimize model parameters, analyze system behavior, and perform advanced mathematical computations on biochemical models.
For parameter estimation workflows using experimental data, see [Parameter Estimation](https://deepwiki.com/copasi/basico/4.1-parameter-estimation). For systematic parameter space exploration, see [Parameter Scanning](https://deepwiki.com/copasi/basico/4.4-parameter-scanning). ## Overview of Optimization Tasks
Basico provides several computational analysis capabilities through task-specific modules, each implementing the standard COPASI task execution pattern of initialization, configuration, execution, and result retrieval.

Basico provides specialized mathematical analysis capabilities for advanced system characterization, including Lyapunov exponent computation for chaos detection and Metabolic Control Analysis for flux control.

keenable.title: Computational Tasks
keenable.snippet:
This document covers the computational task system in basico, which provides a unified interface for running various types of model analysis and simulation methods. Computational tasks represent the core analytical capabilities of basico, enabling users to perform simulations, optimizations, parameter estimation, and specialized analyses on biochemical models.

Basico provides several categories of computational tasks, each addressing different types of model analysis:
| Category | Tasks | Primary Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Simulation** | Time Course, Steady State | Model dynamics and equilibrium analysis |
| **Optimization** | Optimization, Parameter Estimation | Parameter fitting and objective minimization |
| **Analysis** | Sensitivities, MCA, Lyapunov | Model behavior characterization |
| **Exploration** | Parameter Scan, Profile Likelihood | Parameter space investigation |

To perform a basic profile likelihood analysis of a fit obtained, basico implements the [Schaber method](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0303264712001670) that in turn fixes each optimization parameter, while reoptimizing the remaining parameters. This scan is performed in both directions. Ideally, what we would want to see for identified parameters, is that the result gets worse, as we go away from the found solution. If we find a flat line, that means the parameter is not identifiable, if we find a curve that is flat on one side, we can only identify the corresponding bound.
Since this could potentially take quite some time basico breaks this task into three steps:
- generating different copasi models for each of the scans. (these files could then be moved to a cluster environment for parallel computation)
- running the the scans (here basico uses the python mulitiprocessing library), which places reports into a specified directory
- plotting the result, by specifying the directory where the reports have been stashed.

This thesis examines how to best describe the kinetics of β-galactosidase-catalyzed transgalactosylation for producing galactooligosaccharides (GOS) from lactose. The motivation is to obtain reliable models that can predict product distribution and yield, given that β-galactosidase catalyzes both hydrolysis and galactosyl transfer with low product specificity. The work analyzes the mechanistic and mathematical assumptions of selected literature models (including proposals by Boon, Vera, and Palai) and evaluates their performance by fitting them to laboratory time-course data using β-galactosidase from Aspergillus oryzae. Experiments covered two enzyme loadings and three initial lactose concentrations; saccharide profiles were quantified by HPAE-PAD, and parameters were estimated via nonlinear regression using custom Python code and COPASI. ultimate.title: Profile likelihood — basiCO documentation
ultimate.snippet:
To perform a basic profile likelihood analysis of a fit obtained, basico implements the [Schaber method](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0303264712001670) that in turn fixes each optimization parameter, while reoptimizing the remaining parameters. This scan is performed in both directions. Ideally, what we would want to see for identified parameters, is that the result gets worse, as we go away from the found solution. If we find a flat line, that means the parameter is not identifiable, if we find a curve that is flat on one side, we can only identify the corresponding bound.
Since this could potentially take quite some time basico breaks this task into three steps:
- generating different copasi models for each of the scans. (these files could then be moved to a cluster environment for parallel computation)
- running the the scans (here basico uses the python mulitiprocessing library), which places reports into a specified directory
- plotting the result, by specifying the directory where the reports have been stashed.
